answer:
**Merging works best when weight coordinates still mean roughly the same thing.** Two models fine-tuned from one checkpoint start with aligned neurons and features. Small task-specific changes may therefore be combined in a meaningful coordinate system. Two independently trained networks can represent the same function using permuted neurons, making naive coordinate-wise averaging destructive. [1](https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.01708)

A simple example shows the issue. One network uses its first hidden unit for cats and its second for dogs; another swaps those units. Averaging corresponding weights without aligning units mixes unrelated features. Shared initialization reduces this particular mismatch, although long or aggressive fine-tuning can still produce incompatible updates.

Weight averaging interpolates checkpoints. Task arithmetic subtracts the common base to form updates and then adds scaled updates back to that base. SLERP interpolates directions geometrically. TIES trims small updates, resolves sign disagreements, and combines selected contributions. If one task moves a weight upward and another moves it downward, their disagreement is precisely what a merging rule must handle.

**Compatibility is an empirical question.** Shared architecture, tokenizer, and base are practical prerequisites for simple merging, not proof of success. Tune merge coefficients using held-out examples from all desired tasks and compare against each source model. Include retention and failure slices; an average score can hide that one important capability disappeared. A low-loss interpolation path is something to establish, not assume universally.

**Technical details and references.**

Fine-tuned models from the same initialization often preserve parameter alignment, making interpolation or task-vector addition more meaningful than averaging independently initialized networks. Define $\Delta_i=\theta_i-\theta_0$ and merge $\theta=\theta_0+\sum_i\alpha_i\Delta_i$. [1](https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.01708)

Ordinary averaging combines weights directly; task arithmetic combines deltas; SLERP interpolates directions on a sphere; TIES trims small deltas and resolves sign conflicts before merging. These are empirical methods, not guarantees of a low-loss path. Different architectures/tokenizers or neuron permutations can make merging invalid.

Tune coefficients on a held-out multi-task suite and test interference, retention, and safety-relevant behaviors. Do not optimize the merge on the final test set. A merged model can fail tasks that every source checkpoint handled well.
